pages.name: Flux through the coil
pages.text: Two magnet poles face each other, and their field runs straight across from north to south. A coil of wire turns between them, seen end-on, so it shows as a line with a wire at each end. The shaded band is the field passing through the coil, its [[flux]]. Face-on the coil catches the most, edge-on none, and past edge-on the field passes through from the other side. The trace shows the flux as a share of its face-on amount. Drag the ringed wire round.

pages.name: Edge-on
pages.task: The coil is edge-on to the field. How much flux passes through it?
pages.why: Edge-on, the coil's face lies along the field lines, so they all slip past and none passes through. Its flux is zero. Face-on it catches the most, and turned 60° from face-on, half.

pages.name: The emf
pages.text: Now the coil spins steadily. A changing flux makes a push round the coil, its [[emf]], traced below in volts, and the lamp shows the current it drives. The emf is zero where the flux trace is at its top or bottom. It peaks where the flux crosses zero at its steepest, and the short line riding the flux trace shows that slope. The emf is drawn as how fast the flux falls, Faraday's minus sign; which way round counts as positive is a choice.

pages.name: Where it peaks
pages.task: The coil turns steadily. Where in its turn is the emf biggest?
pages.why: The emf follows how fast the flux changes, not how much there is. Edge-on, the flux crosses zero at its steepest, so the emf peaks. Face-on, the flux is at its most and for that instant not changing, like a ball at the top of its throw, so the emf is zero.

pages.name: Why a sine
pages.text: Why a sine? The ringed wire is the arm in From circle to wave, with θ measured from the upright, face-on, so here its height is cos θ, the flux share. It moves round steadily, and only its up-and-down part crosses the field lines and changes the flux: its speed × sin θ. So the emf goes as sin θ, and it reverses each time the coil passes face-on.

pages.name: What reverses
pages.task: Something reverses every half turn, as the coil passes face-on. What is it?
pages.why: As the coil passes face-on, the flux stops falling and starts rising, so the push reverses, and the lamp's current reverses with it. The magnets' field never changes. Current driven to and fro like this is [[alternating current]].

pages.name: Faster
pages.text: Turn the coil faster and its flux changes faster, so the push is bigger. At 2 turns a second the peak doubles to 6.28 V, and each wave takes half as long, 0.5 s. The dashed wave is the coil at 1 turn a second. Slide the speed, and the height and the period change together.
pages.alt: A north pole on the left and a south pole on the right, their field running straight across. The coil is 90 degrees from face-on, and 0 of its face-on flux passes through it. Its emf is 6.28 V, peaking at 6.28 V.

pages.name: Twice as fast
pages.task: The coil turns twice as fast, 2 turns a second instead of 1. What happens to its emf?
pages.answer: Doubles the peak, halves the period
pages.why: Twice as fast, the flux changes twice as fast, so the peak doubles to 6.28 V. Each turn takes half as long, so the period halves to 0.5 s. Speed changes both together.
pages.alt: A wave of emf against time, 3.14 V peak, 1 turn a second. After the change, 6.28 V peak, 2 turns a second.

pages.name: Turns and field
pages.text: Each turn of wire adds its own push, and a stronger field gives more flux to change, so both scale the peak. Neither changes how fast the coil turns, so the period stays at 1 s. With 200 turns of wire the peak doubles to 6.28 V. The dashed wave is the coil with 100 turns at 0.5 T.

pages.name: Three times the turns
pages.task: A coil gives 12 V peak. It is rewound with three times the turns of wire, at the same field and speed. What does it give?
pages.why: Each turn of wire adds its own push, so three times the turns gives 3 × 12 = 36 V. The speed is the same, so each wave takes as long as before.
pages.alt: A wave of emf against time, 12 V peak. After the change, 36 V peak.

pages.name: 30° past face-on
pages.task: Mixed. This coil peaks at 20 V, and it is 30° past face-on. What is its emf now?
pages.why: The emf goes as the sine of the angle from face-on, so it is 20 × sin 30° = 10 V. The cosine gives 17.3 V, which is the shape of the flux, not the emf.

pages.name: 60 Hz at sea
pages.task: Mixed. This simple coil gives 100 V peak at 50 turns a second, a 50 Hz wave. To make 60 Hz it turns 60 times a second, with the same field. What is its peak?
pages.why: The peak follows how fast the flux changes, so turning 60 times a second instead of 50 gives 100 × 60 ÷ 50 = 120 V, at 60 Hz. 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship. A real generator adjusts its field to hold its voltage, which Three-phase power systems at sea takes up.
pages.alt: A wave of emf against time, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. After the change, 120 V peak, 60 Hz.
